title: The power of time reversal in Hamiltonian property testing
authors: Richard R. Allen, Matthias C. Caro, Yanlin Chen, Tom Gur, Angus Lowe
abstract: Quantum algorithms enable Heisenberg-limited scaling across many tasks in sensing and learning, achieving precision $\varepsilon$ using $O(1/\varepsilon)$ total evolution time. However, in Hamiltonian property testing, the best known algorithms have $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ total evolution time, unless it is possible to $\textit{reverse}$ the flow of time under the Hamiltonian. In this work, we prove that time reversal is necessary to close this gap. We establish evolution time lower bounds for Hamiltonian certification and locality testing, for a continuous family of error metrics ranging from average- to worst-case. We also prove matching upper bounds for Hamiltonian certification in all cases, both with and without time reversal, showing that the advantage from time reversal persists. Our results follow from a new Fourier-analytic approach to quantum lower bounds in continuous time, which is sensitive to time reversal and applicable beyond Hamiltonian property testing. This gives an alternative proof that inverses are required for amplitude amplification and estimation, improving the lower bounds of Tang and Wright and extending to fractional queries. We also show that, for unstructured search, uncertainty in the phase of the oracle destroys the quantum speedup without inverse queries, even when the oracle is fixed and coherent. Our work rigorously establishes time reversal as a resource governing both the precision of quantum measurement and the robustness of quantum algorithms.
summary: This paper proves that the ability to reverse time (i.e., access inverse unitary operations) is a necessary resource for achieving optimal quantum speedups in continuous-time tasks like Hamiltonian property testing. Using a new Fourier-analytic technique, the authors establish lower bounds that demonstrate a clear separation in required evolution time when time reversal is unavailable. This work fundamentally characterizes time reversal as a key resource governing quantum measurement precision.
main_problem: The paper investigates the fundamental necessity of time reversal (inverse unitary operations) for achieving optimal scaling in continuous-time quantum tasks like Hamiltonian property testing.
main_result: It rigorously proves that time reversal is a necessary resource, establishing lower bounds for evolution time that are significantly worse without the ability to reverse time.
method: The authors develop a novel Fourier-analytic approach to quantum lower bounds in continuous time, extending techniques from discrete query models.
model_or_system: The study analyzes quantum evolution governed by an unknown Hamiltonian H in a continuous-time setting, applied to problems like Hamiltonian certification and locality testing.
key_observables: Evolution time (T), error metric (ranging from average-case to worst-case), and the distinguishability of Hamiltonians.
important_parameters: Precision ($\epsilon$), Hilbert space dimension ($d$), and the structure of the Hamiltonian (e.g., local vs. global).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes black-box access to time evolution under the unknown Hamiltonian and relies on establishing separations across a continuous family of error metrics.
paper_structure: The work progresses by establishing lower bounds for Hamiltonian certification and locality testing, showing separations between time-reversible and non-time-reversible protocols. It then extends these techniques to provide alternative proofs for the necessity of inverses in amplitude amplification and unstructured search.
why_interesting: The rigorous establishment of time reversal as a fundamental resource governing quantum measurement precision and algorithm robustness provides deep theoretical insights applicable to open quantum systems and time-dependent dynamics.
